A rectangular local-equilibrium field record consists of an open temperature interval $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$, a temperature field $T:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathcal T$ whose time derivative through order one and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times I$, a function $u\in C^1(\mathcal T,\mathbb R)$ of internal-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and its volumetric heat capacity $c(T):=u'(T)>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The coordinates $x_i$ are lengths in metres, and $T$ is measured in kelvins, using [[def-td-si-quantities]].

The record may also include a thermal-energy flux-density field $j_Q:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and a conductivity field $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. For any unit vector $n$, $j_Q\cdot n$ is the signed thermal-energy transfer rate per unit area in direction $n$, positive when energy flows along $n$. The flux and tensor are field data here; no relation between them is imposed by this Definition. In Euclidean coordinates, $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$. The classical divergence $\operatorname{div}j_Q(x,t):=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}(j_Q)_i(x,t)$ is defined at interior points where these three partial derivatives exist. On a flat face, $n$ denotes its outward unit normal.

A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. $$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: Expand the square in the product integral and use [A1]: $\int_\Omega\int_\Omega(w(x)-w(y))^2\,dy\,dx=2|\Omega|\int_\Omega w^2-2(\int_\Omega w)^2=2|\Omega|\int_\Omega w^2$. The integrand is continuous, so [F2] justifies the repeated integrals.

For $x,y\in\Omega$, define $z^{(0)}=x$ and $z^{(i)}=(y_1,\ldots,y_i,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_d)$ for $1\le i\le d$, and set $\delta_i=w(z^{(i-1)})-w(z^{(i)})$. Then $w(x)-w(y)=\sum_i\delta_i$ and $d\sum_i\delta_i^2-(\sum_i\delta_i)^2=\sum_{i<j}(\delta_i-\delta_j)^2\ge0$.

Fix $i$ and the other coordinates. By [F1], $\delta_i$ is the integral of $h=\partial_iw$ over the interval between $x_i$ and $y_i$. If the endpoints differ, let $\bar h$ be the average of $h$ on that interval. Nonnegativity of $\int(h-\bar h)^2$ gives $(\int h)^2\le |x_i-y_i|\int h^2$; if they agree, $\delta_i=0$. Since $|x_i-y_i|\le L_i$, in both cases $\delta_i^2\le L_i\int_0^{L_i}|\partial_iw(z_1,\ldots,z_{i-1},s,z_{i+1},\ldots,z_d)|^2\,ds$.

Integrate the last bound over $x,y$. The $x_i,y_i$ integrations contribute $L_i^2$, the displayed segment bound contributes $L_i$, each unused variable from a pair $x_j,y_j$ with $j\ne i$ contributes $L_j$, and the remaining variables and $s$ give $\int_\Omega|\partial_iw|^2$. By [F2], this yields $\int_\Omega\int_\Omega\delta_i^2\,dy\,dx\le |\Omega|L_i^2\int_\Omega|\partial_iw|^2$.

By step 1.2 and the finite squared-sum inequality, the double integral in step 1.1 is at most $d\sum_i\int_\Omega\int_\Omega\delta_i^2\,dy\,dx$. Apply step 2.1, divide by $2|\Omega|>0$, and use $\sum_iL_i^2|\partial_iw|^2\le(\max_iL_i^2)|\nabla w|^2$ pointwise. This gives both stated inequalities with the displayed $C_\Omega$.

$0<\tau<T<\infty$; $u_t=\Delta u$.

$\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be bounded and

$$ \sup_{x \in K} |(f*K_\varepsilon)(x)-f(x)| \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$

   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n\ge1$ and $t>0$. The **heat kernel on $\mathbb R^n$** is the function

$$\Gamma(x,t):=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{|x|^2}{4t}\Bigr),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n,$$

where $|x|^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ is the Euclidean square of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\exp$ is the real exponential function of

and a scalar multiple, so it is $C^\infty$ in the sense of

strictly positive by [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]. The
spatial Laplacian entering the heat equation is that of

proved for the kernel on this page, and the causal extension is used only as a

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

derivations.claim: The assumptions on $g$ make it bounded and uniformly continuous, so [F1] applies. Write $U(x,\theta)=\Gamma_\theta*g(x)$ and set $T(x,t)=U(x,at)$. The chain rule gives $\partial_tT=aU_\theta(x,at)=a\Delta U(x,at)=a\Delta T$ for $t>0$; [F1] also gives the formula, smoothness, and local uniform initial convergence. Since $k=ac$, this is $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$. With $u'(T)=c$, $u_t=cT_t$, and $j_Q=-k\nabla T$ from [A3, A4], the same equality gives $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}j_Q=c\partial_tT-k\Delta T=0$.

Positivity and unit mass in [F2] imply $T_{\min}\int\Gamma\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}\int\Gamma$, hence $T_{\min}\le T\le T_{\max}$. Translation by $2L_i$ in the convolution variable preserves $g$ and Lebesgue measure by [F6], so $T$ is $2L_i$-periodic in $x_i$. Reflection $y_i\mapsto-y_i$ preserves Lebesgue measure by [F7] because its matrix has determinant of absolute value one; evenness of the kernel [F9] and of $g$ then makes $T$ even in each coordinate. For $t>0$, evenness gives $\partial_{x_i}T=0$ on the face $x_i=0$; periodicity gives $\partial_{x_i}T=\partial_{x_i}T$ at opposite faces $x_i=-L_i,L_i$, while evenness makes these two values negatives, so both vanish. The same boundary derivative holds at $t=0$ for $g$, and [A4] gives $j_Q\cdot n=0$ on every face.

By [F11], the stated $C^2$ hypothesis gives continuous derivatives through spatial order two. For $|\alpha|\le2$ and $t>0$, differentiating under the integral and then integrating by parts in each coordinate gives $D^\alpha T(x,t)=\int\Gamma(x-y,at)D^\alpha g(y)\,dy$. The products of kernel derivatives with bounded derivatives of $g$ are absolutely integrable by the Gaussian bound [F2], so [F10] licenses the iterated integrals; on each finite coordinate interval Newton–Leibniz [F8] gives the integration-by-parts identity, and the boundary terms vanish as the interval expands because of the Gaussian tails. Each $D^\alpha g$ is bounded and continuous, so [F4] makes this expression converge uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ to $D^\alpha g$ as $t\downarrow0$. Thus the spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to the initial time.

For $t>0$, the heat equation and the same integration-by-parts argument give $\partial_tT(x,t)=a\int\Gamma(x-y,at)\Delta g(y)\,dy$. By [F4] this converges uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ to $a\Delta g(x)$. For $0<\varepsilon<t$, [F8] gives $T(x,t)-T(x,\varepsilon)=\int_\varepsilon^t\partial_sT(x,s)\,ds$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ is valid uniformly in $x$ by step 1.1 and the uniform limit just established; consequently $T(x,t)-g(x)=\int_0^t\partial_sT(x,s)\,ds$, and dividing by $t$ proves the right derivative $\partial_tT(x,0)=a\Delta g(x)$.

For uniqueness, let $T_1,T_2$ be two solutions in the stated regularity class and set $w=T_1-T_2$. Then $w_t=a\Delta w$, $\partial_nw=0$, and $w(\cdot,0)=0$. At each fixed time, $w$ and its spatial derivatives through order two are continuous on the compact rectangle, so the integrands $w\,\partial_i^2w$ and $|\partial_iw|^2$ are bounded and hence $L^1$ for the finite Lebesgue product measure. The product rule and [F8] then give $\int_0^{L_i}w\,\partial_i^2w=[w\partial_iw]_0^{L_i}-\int_0^{L_i}|\partial_iw|^2$. The boundary terms vanish by the homogeneous Neumann condition, so $E'(t)=2a\int_\Omega w\Delta w=-2a\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\le0$. Let $L_i>0$ be lengths measured in metres, set $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$, and take the open temperature interval $\mathcal T=(0,\infty)$ with temperatures measured in kelvins. Fix a constant volumetric heat capacity $c>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$, a constant scalar conductivity $k>0$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, and an arbitrary reference energy density $u_\star$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. Define $u:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R$ by $u(\theta)=u_\star+c\theta$, so $u'(\theta)=c$, and define $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ by $K(x,\theta)=kI_3$ as in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]]. Put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

Let $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathcal T$ be $C^2$ and satisfy, for every $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$g(x_1,\ldots,-x_i,\ldots,x_3)=g(x_1,\ldots,x_i,\ldots,x_3),\qquad g(x_1,\ldots,x_i+2L_i,\ldots,x_3)=g(x_1,\ldots,x_i,\ldots,x_3).$$
Assume every coordinate derivative $D^\alpha g$ with $|\alpha|\le2$ is bounded and uniformly continuous, and that $0<T_{\min}\le g(y)\le T_{\max}<\infty$ for all $y$, with these bounds measured in kelvins.

For $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$. Here $y$ is measured in metres, $\theta=at$ in the kernel has units $\mathrm{m^2}$, and the normalized kernel $\Gamma(\cdot,at)$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, so the integral has units of kelvins. Also $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$, $\Delta T:=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2T$, and on a face with outward unit normal $n$, $\partial_nT:=n\cdot\nabla T$. For every finite $\tau>0$, this is the unique function $T$ continuous on $\overline\Omega\times[0,\tau]$ whose first time derivative for $t>0$ and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times[0,\tau]$, solving $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega\times(0,\tau]$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on each face and the given initial value. The time derivative at $t=0$ is interpreted from the right. The field satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, its spatial derivatives through order two are continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$.

On $I=(0,\infty)$, set $j_Q(x,t)=-k\nabla T(x,t)$. Then $(T,u,j_Q,K)$ is a field record of [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]] satisfying [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], so the solution is global in time for this restricted physical continuum model.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be lengths in metres, and set $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with closure $\overline\Omega$. A rectangular local-equilibrium field record consists of an open temperature interval $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$, a temperature field $T:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathcal T$ whose time derivative through order one and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times I$, a function $u\in C^1(\mathcal T,\mathbb R)$ of internal-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and its volumetric heat capacity $c(T):=u'(T)>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The coordinates $x_i$ are lengths in metres, and $T$ is measured in kelvins, using [[def-td-si-quantities]].

The record may also include a thermal-energy flux-density field $j_Q:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and a conductivity field $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. For any unit vector $n$, $j_Q\cdot n$ is the signed thermal-energy transfer rate per unit area in direction $n$, positive when energy flows along $n$. The flux and tensor are field data here; no relation between them is imposed by this Definition. In Euclidean coordinates, $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$ and $\operatorname{div}j_Q=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}(j_Q)_i$. On a flat face, $n$ denotes its outward unit normal.

This is a specified regular field class on a fixed rigid body. It does not assert that every physical medium has local-equilibrium fields, nor does it adopt a heat equation, a boundary condition, Fourier's law, or an entropy-production law.

For a field record on $\Omega\times I$ from [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt the local balance
$$\partial_t u(T(x,t))+\operatorname{div}j_Q(x,t)=0$$
and the insulated-boundary condition $j_Q(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ on every face of $\partial\Omega$. Both terms in the local equation have units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$. The boundary condition says that no heat energy crosses the body's outer faces in this model.

This local continuum balance is an additional adopted postulate, with the sign and energy convention of [[post-td-first-law-energy]]. It is not deduced from that global process-record balance. Matter transfer, volume work, internal sources, moving boundaries, and external-field energy require separately specified balance models and are outside this item.

$$j_Q(x,t)=-K(x,T(x,t))\nabla T(x,t).$$
Here $K$ has entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $j_Q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, so the equation is dimensionally consistent. Write $K_s=(K+K^{\mathsf T})/2$ for the symmetric part and assume $z^{\mathsf T}K_s(x,T)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. The antisymmetric part may contribute to the flux but not to the quadratic entropy production.

This is an adopted constitutive model in the stated continuum regime. It is neither a consequence of equilibrium entropy alone nor a universal law for all media. In particular, it does not assert a finite propagation speed or an empirical value for $K$.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be bounded and
continuous. Then for every compact set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$ \sup_{x \in K} |(f*K_\varepsilon)(x)-f(x)| \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $n\ge1$ and $t>0$. The **heat kernel on $\mathbb R^n$** is the function

$$\Gamma(x,t):=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{|x|^2}{4t}\Bigr),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n,$$

where $|x|^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ is the Euclidean square of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\exp$ is the real exponential function of
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]. For fixed $t>0$ the map
$x\mapsto\Gamma(x,t)$ is a composite of the quadratic form with the exponential
and a scalar multiple, so it is $C^\infty$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] by
[[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and
[[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]], and it is
strictly positive by [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]. The
spatial Laplacian entering the heat equation is that of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

The **causal extension** of the heat kernel is $\Gamma(x,t)$ for $t>0$ and
$\Gamma(x,t):=0$ for $t\le0$; the displayed formula is not evaluated at $t=0$
as a function value. The normalisation is fixed by the unit-mass identity
proved for the kernel on this page, and the causal extension is used only as a
locally integrable function or, after embedding, as a distribution.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$
and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling:
$\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there,
$\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$
there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with
$|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for
all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and
$(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and uniformly continuous. Define
$u(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)u_0(y)\,dy$ for $t>0$ and
$u(x,0):=u_0(x)$. Then $u$ is $C^\infty$ on

uniformly at the initial time:
$\sup_{x\in K}|u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$ for every compact
$K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Countable Choice is inherited by Gaussian normalization, differentiation, heat Cauchy solution and reflection change of variables. Positive bounded even-periodic C2 g has all bounded uniformly continuous derivatives through order two. Convolution at a=k/c solves T_t=a Delta T; positivity/unit mass preserves bounds. Let $L_i>0$ be lengths measured in metres, set $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$, and take the open temperature interval $\mathcal T=(0,\infty)$ with temperatures measured in kelvins. Fix a constant volumetric heat capacity $c>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$, a constant scalar conductivity $k>0$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, and an arbitrary reference energy density $u_\star$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. Define $u:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R$ by $u(\theta)=u_\star+c\theta$, so $u'(\theta)=c$, and define $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ by $K(x,\theta)=kI_3$ as in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]]. Put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

Let $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathcal T$ be $C^2$ and satisfy, for every $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$g(x_1,\ldots,-x_i,\ldots,x_3)=g(x_1,\ldots,x_i,\ldots,x_3),\qquad g(x_1,\ldots,x_i+2L_i,\ldots,x_3)=g(x_1,\ldots,x_i,\ldots,x_3).$$
Assume every coordinate derivative $D^\alpha g$ with $|\alpha|\le2$ is bounded and uniformly continuous, and that $0<T_{\min}\le g(y)\le T_{\max}<\infty$ for all $y$, with these bounds measured in kelvins.

For $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$. Here $y$ is measured in metres, $\theta=at$ in the kernel has units $\mathrm{m^2}$, and the normalized kernel $\Gamma(\cdot,at)$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, so the integral has units of kelvins. Also $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$, $\Delta T:=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2T$, and on a face with outward unit normal $n$, $\partial_nT:=n\cdot\nabla T$. For every finite $\tau>0$, this is the unique function $T$ continuous on $\overline\Omega\times[0,\tau]$ whose first time derivative for $t>0$ and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times[0,\tau]$, solving $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega\times(0,\tau]$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on each face and the given initial value. The time derivative at $t=0$ is interpreted from the right. The field satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, its spatial derivatives through order two are continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$.

On $I=(0,\infty)$, set $j_Q(x,t)=-k\nabla T(x,t)$. Then $(T,u,j_Q,K)$ is a field record of [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]] satisfying [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], so the solution is global in time for this restricted physical continuum model.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
